content.thinking:
I need to piece together the causal chain without using specific numeric figures directly—using placeholders instead. The story starts with users experiencing slow account pages, tied to a HighLatency alert where latency climbed substantially while error rates only rose modestly, peaking at a higher level.

For the "why," I'm attributing the issue to capacity saturation—three replicas getting overwhelmed by traffic—citing the relevant log and ticket evidence, and noting that this is confirmed by the fix: scaling out resolved it and latency returned to baseline. I want to be careful to cite the actual record entries rather than treating metric readings as standalone facts, hedging where the traffic growth interpretation comes from the investigator's reading rather than something independently verified.

For contributing factors, I'm flagging that there was no autoscaling or capacity headroom configured—this is unknown/unverified but worth an action item—and noting the detection gap where the alert fired after onset and was mislabeled as latency when it was really about error rate. I'll recommend action items around adding capacity-based alerting and earlier detection, making sure to tie these back to specific ticket references.

Settling on the root cause: traffic on io-shop grew beyond what the fixed three replicas could handle, saturating CPU and driving up latency, with no deploy or config change responsible. I'm defining AI-3 (enable autoscaling or raise baseline replica count with headroom) and AI-4 (alert on CPU saturation or traffic surge before latency becomes critical), and noting the time-to-alert metric from onset to alert_raised.

For the executive summary, I'll fill placeholders for the slow-page duration, error rate climbing from a baseline to its worst point, Argus's replica addition, and the recovery and closure times. On what went well versus poorly: Argus caught the signal quickly and scaling resolved things fast, but alert latency after onset was a gap, and the fix PR being a code change for what's fundamentally a capacity issue seems like a mismatch worth flagging.

action_items.item: Enable autoscaling for io-shop on CPU and request load, and set a minimum replica count with headroom above the recent peak, so a demand rise adds capacity without manual action.
Add an early-warning alert on io-shop CPU utilisation approaching its limit and on a sustained rise in request volume, so the team hears about saturation before latency and errors climb.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw slow account pages and a slightly higher share of failed requests. The latency series behind the alert went from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average and peaked at {series_at_worst}. The error rate went from {errors_before} to a peak of {errors_at_worst}. The warning logs report the elevated page error rate, and many failures were shoppers closing the connection, which fits waiting on slow pages.

The replicas serving io-shop could not handle the load they were getting, so requests queued and latency rose. Scaling the deployment out was the only action taken, and the service returned to baseline from {recovered} once it was confirmed. This points to a shortage of capacity and not a fault in the code.
The service was running on a fixed set of replicas, and that capacity had been outgrown by the load. The deployment was scaled out from {T21.2} replicas.

Nothing else changed that could explain the onset. No production changes were recorded in the hours before the incident, and the flag provider showed no recent flag changes. The remaining difference is the load on the service against its fixed capacity.

contributing_factors.factor: Capacity for io-shop was a fixed replica count with no evidence of automatic scaling or headroom, so a rise in demand turned directly into user-facing latency until someone scaled it by hand.

Detection came late and from a symptom. The page was raised at {alert_raised}, which is {alert_raised - began} after the onset at {began}. Nothing warned earlier that traffic was climbing or that CPU was nearing its limit.
The only open follow-up is a draft pull request, but the record shows a capacity shortage with no code or config change. It is not clear that the pull request addresses the cause.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, from {began} to {recovered}, shop account pages were slow, and a small extra share of requests failed. The error rate went from {errors_before} before the incident to {errors_while_broken} on average, and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. The latency measure behind the page went from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average, and peaked at {series_at_worst}. The service had no recent change. It was short of capacity for the load it was getting. Argus added replicas, and the service was back at its baseline from {recovered}. Argus closed the incident at {closed}. The response took {held}, which is not the length of the outage. A draft pull request was also opened, and it is still awaiting review.

got_lucky: The extra failures were small next to the baseline error rate, so few shoppers were hurt. A larger surge on the same fixed capacity could have been much worse.
Scaling out worked at once. Had the extra replicas been unavailable, such as when GPU nodes are scarce, recovery would have been slower.
went_well: Argus read the metrics, change events, flag history and logs within seconds, and ruled out a deploy or flag change as the cause.
The scale-out was confirmed against the service's own metrics, and the paging rule stopped firing.
went_wrong: The page came {alert_raised - began} after the onset, so users were affected before anyone was told.
The alert name speaks of latency while its text speaks of error rate, which makes it harder to read at a glance.
The follow-up is a code-fix pull request for what the record shows as a capacity problem.

input.root_cause: Demand on io-shop outgrew the capacity of its fixed set of replicas, which ran out of CPU headroom and slowed down. No deploy, release or flag change was involved, and adding replicas cleared the problem.
input.symptom: Account pages were slow and some requests failed
